title: Object-Oriented Programming in R
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of object-oriented programming in r and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply overview of r's object systems in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Object-Oriented Programming in R is part of Advanced R Programming and Performance. Start with overview of r's object systems and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: Advanced R behavior is easier to reason about by inspecting semantics and measuring representative workloads instead of guessing.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Advanced R behavior is easier to reason about by inspecting semantics and measuring representative workloads instead of guessing. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: State the expected behavior, compare equivalent implementations and measure before optimizing. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Object-Oriented Programming in R
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 224: Object-Oriented Programming in R
answer <- local({ temporary <- 2; temporary * temporary })
answer
content_blocks.run_instructions: CodeLeaf does not provide an R runtime. This block is an inspectable reference example; execute it in a local R console or a reviewed R-aware environment. Static validation checks file structure, not R semantics.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No example is executed by this CodeLeaf lesson. For a local run, use synthetic data in a temporary working directory, avoid production credentials or destructive writes, and restart a clean R session to clear lesson objects.
content_blocks.limitations: Profile representative workloads before optimizing and verify identical outputs across implementations. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For object-oriented programming in r, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

content.task: Apply object-oriented programming in r to a small synthetic example. Start with overview of r's object systems, predict the result, compare it with a local R run, test one edge or failure case, and document one limitation. For integrations or package-dependent topics, submit a safe verification plan rather than claiming the code ran.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the overview of r's object systems idea in a minimal example or safe design sketch.
State the expected result before running the example.
Verify one relevant boundary, missing-value or failure case.
Record assumptions and one limitation of the result.
content.expected_output: A reproducible object-oriented programming in r example or design sketch with the expected result, one checked edge or failure case, and a stated limitation.
hints: Start with “Overview of R's Object Systems” and identify the input and output before coding.
Prefer a small repeatable test and capture the result before changing the implementation.
Test a boundary, missing, invalid or failure input relevant to this topic.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
